title: What a fraction really is
hook: Cut a 6 m length of cable into 2 m tails and you get three; cut it into three-quarter-metre tails and you get eight. How can dividing by a fraction make a number bigger?
oneBreath: A fraction is one number with its own place on the line, like the three-quarter mark on a tape. Its bottom number names the size of piece and its top counts those pieces, so one number can wear many names, and once two fractions are written in the same piece size, comparing, adding and taking away is just counting pieces. Multiplying by a fraction takes a part of a part, and dividing by one asks how many of that piece fit, which is why a small piece gives a big count.

ideas.title: A fraction is one number
ideas.oneLine: Three-quarters of an inch is one number with its own mark on the tape, not two numbers stuck together, and so is one and three-quarters.

ideas.title: Equal pieces make the bottom number honest
ideas.oneLine: The bottom number counts the equal pieces in a whole, the top counts yours, so a piece is a quarter only if all four match.

ideas.title: More pieces means smaller pieces
ideas.oneLine: Splitting one whole into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller, so a tenth is less than a fifth although 10 is more than 5.

ideas.title: One number, many names
ideas.oneLine: Cutting every piece into the same number of smaller pieces renames a fraction without moving it, so 3/8 and 6/16 of an inch match.

ideas.title: Compare by matching the piece size
ideas.oneLine: To order imperial drill sizes such as 3/8 and 5/16, rename both in a piece that measures each exactly, sixteenths, and then the tops decide.

ideas.title: Only matching pieces add or take away
ideas.oneLine: Half an hour and three-quarters of an hour add or take away only once both are counted in quarters, and then only the tops add.

ideas.title: A fraction of a fraction multiplies
ideas.oneLine: Half of three-quarters of a circuit's load is three-eighths: tops by tops and bottoms by bottoms, because the second cut runs across pieces already cut.

ideas.title: Dividing by a fraction counts what fits
ideas.oneLine: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of that piece fit into the number, so dividing by less than one gives more, not less.

calibration.q: A 12 m cable is cut into three pieces: 3 m, 4 m and 5 m. What fraction of the cable is the 3 m piece?
options: No fraction fits, because the pieces are not equal
calibration.why: A quarter: 3 m is one of four equal 3 m lengths that make 12 m, whatever the other cuts were. "A third" counts the pieces instead of measuring them; and unequal pieces still have fractions, just not a third each.

calibration.q: Which is closer to a whole: seven-eighths or five-sixths?
options: They are the same distance from a whole
calibration.why: Both are one piece short of a whole, but an eighth is a smaller piece than a sixth, so seven-eighths is missing less and sits closer to one. "The same distance" counts the missing pieces (one each) without noticing the pieces are different sizes.
